summary: This note covers effects of the 1973 oil crisis, focusing on how it shaped the automobile market and Japan's diplomatic position. It describes the shift toward smaller, fuel-efficient Japanese imports and the later responses of Japanese automakers to 1981 export restraints. It also explains Japan's dependence on Middle Eastern oil, its November 1973 move toward the Arab position, and the October 1973 Arab attack on Israel that drove oil prices up.
one_line: Overview of the 1973 oil crisis's effects on car demand, Japanese automakers, Japan's Middle East policy, and the Yom Kippur War's oil price impact.
key_facts: The 1973 oil crisis reduced demand for large cars in the United States.

Japanese imports such as the Toyota Corona, Toyota Corolla, Datsun B210, Honda Civic and Subaru DL had four cylinder engines that were more fuel efficient than typical American V8 and six cylinder engines.
Japanese imports became mass-market leaders with unibody construction and front-wheel drive, which became de facto standards.
Toyota and Nissan (then known as Datsun) introduced larger cars such as the Toyota Cressida, Mazda 616 and Datsun 810 in response to buyer complaints about the small size of first Japanese compacts.
A decade after the 1973 oil crisis, Honda, Toyota and Nissan, affected by the 1981 voluntary export restraints, opened US assembly plants.
Honda, Toyota and Nissan established luxury divisions Acura, Lexus and Infiniti, respectively, to distinguish themselves from their mass-market brands.
Japan was the country most dependent on Arab oil, with 71% of its imported oil coming from the Middle East in 1970.
On November 7, 1973, the Saudi and Kuwaiti governments declared Japan a "nonfriendly" country to encourage it to change its noninvolvement policy.
Japan received a 5% production cut in December, causing a panic.
On November 22, Japan issued a statement asserting that Israel should withdraw from all of the 1967 territories and advocating Palestinian self-determination.
By December 25, Japan was considered an Arab-friendly state.
On October 6, 1973, Syria and Egypt, with support from other Arab nations, launched a surprise attack on Israel on Yom Kippur.
At the time, Iran was the world's second-largest oil exporter and a close US ally.
The Shah of Iran said that oil prices were going to rise and that Western nations had increased the price of wheat sold to Iran by 300 percent.
The Shah of Iran said that it was only fair that oil should cost "ten times more".
